Article Title: Quote of the day by Sam Altman: “Great execution is at least 10 times more important and…” - the lesson behind turning ideas into reality
Article Text:
Quote of the day by Sam Altman

“Great execution is at least 10 times more important and a 100 times harder than a good idea.”

What Sam Altman’s quote means

Why a good idea is only the beginning

The difficult work that customers rarely see

Sam Altman’s experience with startups

Execution is not the same as simply working harder

Feedback changes the original idea

The misconception that the best idea always wins

What the quote can teach about work and business

Where a good idea meets reality

Lessons from Sam Altman’s quote

Ideas are only the starting point — A good idea still needs testing and development.

Start before it feels perfect — Early action brings useful feedback sooner.

Learn from mistakes — Failures can reveal what needs to change.

Stay flexible — Be ready to adjust the original plan when needed.

Focus on steady improvement — Small changes can strengthen the final result.

Work with direction — Effort matters most when focused on the right problems.

Listen to customers — Real users can expose weaknesses and reveal what matters.

Expect the first version to change — The final product may look very different from the original idea.

Keep improving after launch — Execution does not stop once a product is released.

Give the process time — Turning an idea into something useful takes patience and persistence.

A good idea can arrive quickly that might come from a problem someone notices at work, an inconvenience experienced every day or a simple thought that suddenly seems worth pursuing. At that stage, there is little to lose. The idea can be discussed, changed or abandoned without much consequence. The difficult part starts when someone decides to build it.That is where the difference between having an idea and making something work becomes clear. A product has to be developed, tested, improved and eventually placed in front of real people. Plans encounter practical limits, customers behave differently than expected and mistakes become part of the process. For entrepreneurs and businesses, the distance between an appealing concept and a working result can be considerable. Sam Altman captured this distinction in a widely cited observation about the value of execution.The statement puts the emphasis on the part of entrepreneurship that tends to receive less attention. Ideas are easy to describe.Execution is where the complicated work begins.For Altman, the difference is not simply about putting in more hours. Execution involves turning an uncertain concept into something tangible, learning from what happens and continuing to make decisions as circumstances change.At its simplest, the quote suggests that an idea is only the starting point. Its value becomes clearer when someone can turn it into a useful product, service or business. Consider two people who have almost the same business idea. One spends months discussing possibilities, trying to make every detail perfect before starting. The other builds a basic version, puts it in front of customers and learns from their reactions.The second person may discover that the original plan needs to change. That is not necessarily a failure but an information.Execution brings those discoveries into the open. It forces an idea to deal with costs, technical problems, customer expectations, competition and countless small decisions that cannot be fully anticipated at the beginning.Ideas can look remarkably convincing when there are no constraints around them. A founder can imagine an elegant product, a large audience and a straightforward route to growth. Once development begins, the assumptions underneath that picture have to be tested.Perhaps customers do not consider the problem important enough to pay for a solution. Perhaps the technology is more difficult to build than expected. Perhaps a competitor already offers something similar at a lower price.None of those issues necessarily appear when the idea is first discussed.Execution is the stage at which those questions become unavoidable.People usually encounter the finished product rather than the process that produced it.Behind an application or service may be months of prototypes, revisions, technical fixes and decisions about what should be removed. Some features are tested and abandoned. Others are redesigned several times before they become useful.There is also work that has little to do with the original idea itself. Teams need to recruit people, manage budgets, support customers, maintain technology and deal with problems that appear after launch.As a company grows, those responsibilities generally increase rather than disappear. The polished result can make the journey look much simpler than it actually was.Altman’s view has been shaped by years spent around early-stage companies.He founded Loopt, a location-based social networking company, before becoming involved with Y Combinator. He became president of the startup accelerator in 2014, after previously working with the organisation as a partner.That role exposed him to a large number of founders at the earliest stages of their companies. Many arrived with ambitious ideas. The difficult question was what happened when those ideas met customers, technology and the realities of running a business.Altman later became closely associated with OpenAI, where he served as chief executive. His career has included experience as a founder, investor, startup adviser and technology executive.There is an important distinction in Altman’s statement. Good execution does not necessarily mean doing everything faster or working longer hours. A team can spend enormous amounts of time building the wrong product.The more useful form of execution involves making informed decisions, identifying weaknesses and changing direction when evidence suggests that the original approach is not working.Sometimes the best decision is to stop building a particular feature. At other times, it may mean changing the target customer or simplifying the product. That requires judgement as much as effort.Once a product reaches real users, the original concept often starts to change.Customers may use it in unexpected ways. A feature that seemed central might receive little attention, while a small part of the product becomes surprisingly useful. Complaints can reveal problems that internal testing failed to uncover.For a company willing to listen, those reactions become part of the development process.The original idea does not have to remain untouched. In many cases, the ability to modify it is part of good execution.Business history rarely works as neatly as stories about invention suggest. Several companies can have similar ideas at roughly the same time. Yet only some manage to build products that customers adopt widely. Factors such as distribution, reliability, timing, pricing, management and customer experience can determine what happens after the initial concept.Being first can help, but it does not guarantee that a company will remain ahead.An idea may open the door. The ability to develop it, adapt it and operate it effectively can determine whether the opportunity lasts.Altman’s observation is useful beyond startups. For an individual working on a project, the same principle can apply. Planning has a purpose, but eventually the plan has to be tested. A business proposal needs customers. A new product needs users. A new process needs to work in practice rather than only on paper.That does not mean every idea deserves immediate action. Some ideas should be rejected early. Others need more preparation.The useful distinction is between thinking about an idea indefinitely and creating enough of it to learn whether the idea works.A strong idea can provide direction, but execution gives it a chance to become real. That means paying attention to details, responding to evidence, fixing mistakes and accepting that the finished product may look different from the original plan. It also means understanding that progress can involve stopping, simplifying or starting again.The first version of an idea is rarely the final version.That is why Altman places such a large difference between the two. Thinking of something is often the shortest part of the journey. Building it, testing it, improving it and making it work for other people is where most of the difficulty lies.
Article Summary: Sam Altman’s quote suggests that an idea is only the starting point. Its value becomes clearer when someone can turn it into a useful product, service or business. Execution involves turning an uncertain concept into something tangible, learning from what happens and continuing to make decisions.

Article Title: India's AI Moment: Can We Lead the Future?
Article Text:
By Pravin Kaushal, writer is tech and social entrepreneur

Every year, around this date, we tell ourselves that India is young, hungry and unstoppable. The average Indian is 29. We are an economy of four trillion dollars with a stated ambition of reaching thirty trillion by 2047. The energy is not in question.Look at how that energy is spent. Lakhs of students give three to five years, and their families give their savings, to a single ranked list. Whole towns exist to service that list. The discipline involved is extraordinary, the kind of sustained effort that builds companies and wins wars. And at the end of it, what is produced is a rank. A rank is a private good. It changes one household's trajectory and leaves the country roughly where it was.That is the waste worth talking about this Independence Day. Not a lack of ambition, but ambition pointed at a target too small to matter.Redefine the finish line. Suppose the highest honour at the end of a degree went not to the highest scorer, but to the student who had built the most useful thing. Not necessarily a technology company. A repair service. A crop advisory in the local dialect. A better process for a district office.A piece of software, a product, a village level fix, a social solution. Anything that another human being actually uses.The instrument here is not idealism, it is competition. When nothing else moves Indian students, competition does. We already know it works. We have simply been aiming it at marks instead of at usefulness.The evaluation problem solves itself. The usual objection to any alternative to exams is that it invites manipulation. In practice, the opposite is true. In work done out in the world, the market decides value, users decide usefulness, and impact is visible. A mark sheet can be gamed in ways that a hundred paying customers cannot. And failure is not wasted: a student whose venture collapses has still learnt execution, selling, resilience and leadership, none of which appear on a transcript, all of which an employer will pay for.Artificial intelligence has made this urgent rather than idealistic. The lecture is no longer scarce. A student with a phone can hear the best explanation of any subject on earth, in the language of their choice, and interrogate it at midnight until it makes sense. What remains scarce is judgement, domain depth, context and the ability to make something work in Indian conditions. Universities will matter less for delivering information and more for certifying learning and doing research. The sensible response is to unbundle: study while working, work while studying, return to reskill at forty and again at fifty five, because most of us will be fit to work well into our seventies.The jobs argument deserves a plain answer. Technology has disrupted work repeatedly, through the automobile, electricity and the computer, and each time created more work than it destroyed, though of a kind nobody could have named in advance. The risk is not mass idleness. It is a transition mismanaged: skills that expire faster than institutions can update, and gains captured by a narrow few. That is a design problem, and design problems have owners.Which is where evidence must discipline enthusiasm. We have been here before. A decade and a half ago, one laptop per child was going to transform learning; state schemes were launched with fanfare and shut within a year. The lesson is not cynicism. It is that a technology working in a lab tells us nothing about whether it works in a classroom in Bihar.Where we have bothered to measure, the results are encouraging. A state government's adaptive learning programme, now in more than fifteen hundred schools, doubled the pace of student learning with about an hour of use a week, and only after usage data was fed back to officials who chased down the schools that had gone quiet. Monsoon forecasts built on AI reached tens of millions of farmers, who changed what they planted. Automated testing for driving licences, now running across dozens of transport offices, is associated with a twenty to thirty per cent fall in reports of unsafe driving. None of this is magic. All of it was checked.The sovereignty question. In the last technology cycle, Indians built brilliantly and Indian institutions captured little. Our search, our social platforms and our advertising rents largely belong to others. If, five years from now, no application works without an inference engine, and every inference engine is foreign owned, we will have repeated the mistake at higher cost. The answer is not decoupling. It is capability: models trained here, in our languages, on our data, and equally, AI in the hands of ordinary citizens, not only of the firms that employ them. Large Indian companies could begin by committing one per cent of profits to building AI capability within the company. Most spend more than that on rebranding.Seventy nine years ago, freedom was won by people doing work nobody had assigned them. That instinct is the inheritance worth claiming. A nation of 140 crore people should not be content to produce degree holders. It should produce builders. Change the definition of topper, and watch what a competitive country does with it.
Article Summary: The instrument here is not idealism, it is competition. When nothing else moves Indian students, competition does. We have simply been aiming it at marks instead of at usefulness. Universities will matter less for delivering information and more for certifying learning and doing research.

Article Title: In 2021, Vishal Garg, CEO of $7 billion company fired 900 people on Zoom call; five years later he has been sacked; read 'termination letter'
Article Text:
Representative Image

When Vishal Garg fired 900 employees on a Zoom call, just days before Christmas break

What Better Home & Finance Holding said on Vishal Garg's termination

Vishal Garg sends letter to shareholder asking them to get his CEO job back

US-based Better Home & Finance Holding Company has announced that it terminated founder Vishal Garg as CEO and accused him of delaying the company’s quarterly filing, sharply escalating a dispute over control of the mortgage lender. The statement comes just a day after Garg demanded that five directors resign and claimed majority shareholder support for the proposed board overhaul. Better said that every director other than Garg unanimously voted to terminate him after developing concerns about his "judgment, temperament and credibility."The board also accused Garg of refusing to follow the company’s established shareholder-governance process and said that it would not voluntarily return control to him. Incidentally, the statement contradicts Better’s August 3 announcement that Garg had “mutually agreed” with the board to transition out of the CEO role.In December 201, just days before Christmas, Garg made headlines for laying off 900 employees during a Zoom call. More precisely, on December 6, 2021, Garg announced that the mortgage company is laying off about 9% of its workforce during a Zoom webinar, abruptly informing the more than 900 employees on the call.“If you’re on this call, you are part of the unlucky group that is being laid off,” Garg said on the call. “Your employment here is terminated effective immediately. ” He then said employees could expect an email from HR detailing benefits and severance.Garg cited market efficiency, performance and productivity as the reason behind the firings. The episode also included a leaked email in which Garg referred to employees as “dumb dolphins.” “You are TOO DAMN SLOW. You are a bunch of DUMB DOLPHINS… SO STOP IT. STOP IT. STOP IT RIGHT NOW. YOU ARE EMBARRASSING ME,” Garg reportedly wrote. He subsequently took a monthlong leave while Better’s board commissioned a leadership and cultural assessment, then returned as CEO in January 2022.The Board of Directors (the “Board”), excluding Mr. Garg, unanimously voted to terminate Mr. Garg as Chief Executive Officer following a series of decisions and actions that raised serious concerns regarding his judgment, temperament and credibility. Together with Mr. Garg’s track record—including cumulative GAAP net losses exceeding $1.5 billion since 2022 and a stock price that had declined more than 90% under his leadership—the Board concluded that Mr. Garg was no longer fit to serve in an executive capacity at the Company.Mr. Garg himself told the Board that the Company would have been better off had the capital raised under his leadership simply been invested in U.S. Treasury securities rather than deployed under his stewardship.To get his job back, Vishal Garg has hired the high-profile lawyer Alex Spiro, partner at Quinn Emanuel, to represent him. He has also sent a letter to the board demanding it return him as CEO. He says that he will work for $1 a year until he returns the company to profitability, and that he will transition out of the CEO role afterwards. “It’s an acknowledgment that I’ve been doing this for 10 years, but execution hasn’t been perfect,” Garg said. “I hope it gets resolved. I think the future still remains very bright for Better,” Garg wrote in the letter.
Article Summary: Better Home & Finance Holding Company terminated founder Vishal Garg as CEO. The statement comes just a day after Garg demanded that five directors resign. In December 201, just days before Christmas, Garg made headlines for laying off 900 employees during a Zoom call.

Article Title: In 1830s, real estate agents used Cosmorama gallery to give wealthy 'virtual walkthrough' of fancy mansions; here's how technology worked
Article Text:
Cosmorama Technology (AI-generated image for representational purpose)

Why cosmorama technology worked for real estate

How real estate agents used cosmoramas

Decades ago, rich homebuyers viewed properties through a certain lens. In the 1830s, London estate agents used a technology called the cosmorama to give wealthy buyers a form of “virtual walkthrough” of mansions and country estates. A new study published in the journal Early Popular Visual Culture found evidence that the technology was being used for commercial real estate listings as early as 1838.​The cosmorama allowed prospective buyers to view magnified and illuminated paintings of properties and their surrounding grounds through a lens. Estate agents Brooks and Hedger, later known as Brooks and Green, advertised these cosmoramic views as a way for buyers to inspect distant properties without immediately travelling to them.​“Its great advantages over mere verbal description, is that a purchaser, intent on visiting a distant property may thus enjoy the advantage of having it brought, as it were, within his view, or of selecting for inspection from amongst many, that which best suits his taste and fortune,” one newspaper advertisement said.Cosmoramas emerged in Paris in 1808 and became more widely used during the 1820s. The displays typically consisted of detailed paintings that viewers examined through magnifying lenses.The lens altered how the images appeared, creating a sense of depth and allowing viewers to see distant locations in greater detail.​The technology was primarily used for visual entertainment. People could use cosmoramas to view scenes of cities, landscapes and places far from their homes. The format offered a way to see locations that many viewers would otherwise have been unable to visit.John Plunkett, a professor at the University of Exeter and co-author of the study, was researching 19th-century English cosmoramas when he found a newspaper advertisement from Brooks and Hedger dated to 1838. The estate agency said it offered cosmoramic views of properties available for sale.The advertisements described views showing mansions and their surrounding estates from a bird’s-eye perspective. Creating the images required artists to visit the properties and paint the scenes by hand before they could be displayed through the cosmorama.Brooks and Hedger continued offering the service for nearly two decades, with most of the advertisements found by Plunkett dating from the 1840s. One advertisement described a property view as showing the mansion and estate with “all the vividness and truth of nature.”Because producing each image required considerable work, the service was aimed at expensive properties and country estates.The use of cosmoramas for property sales coincided with changes in the 19th-century real estate market. Population growth and urbanisation increased demand for property, while improvements in transport made it easier for people to travel between locations.The emergence of specialised estate agents also changed how properties were marketed. Instead of relying only on written descriptions, agents could use visual material to show prospective buyers what a distant property looked like.Plunkett said the commercial use of cosmoramas showed how the technology could be adapted beyond entertainment.“What we’ve discovered through this latest research project, however, is that its use extended beyond simple entertainment: the appeal of cosmoramas was that they sold an experience of virtual travel,” Plunkett said in a statement. “This was utilised by estate agents seeking to sell luxury properties and country estates.”The property advertisements therefore provided an early example of estate agents using visual technology to let prospective buyers examine properties remotely. The approach predates modern online listings, panoramic images and virtual reality tours by more than a century.“But the founding of the first specialised estate agents set in motion a more professional approach to marketing property, fuelled by population growth, urbanisation and improved transport links,” Plunkett added. “In that context, we can see how Brooks and Green pioneered the virtual tour, over 150 years before digital technology would fully realise this potential.”
Article Summary: The cosmorama allowed prospective buyers to view magnified and illuminated paintings of properties and their surrounding grounds through a lens. Estate agents Brooks and Hedger, later known as Brooks and Green, advertised these cosmoramic views as a way for buyers to inspect distant properties without immediately travelling to them.

Article Title: SpaceX closes $60 billion Cursor deal: CEO Elon Musk calls it ‘honour’
Article Text:
Here is Cursor’s full announcement

Cursor has officially been acquired by SpaceX. This completes the acquisition process that started in April, when we announced our partnership with SpaceXAI to accelerate our model training efforts.

In the years since we started Cursor, better models have steadily expanded what people can build. Cursor has gone from completing the next few lines of code to building AI teammates that you can give real work to.

Together with SpaceX, we will push that ambition further. We will have access to the largest fleet of GPUs in the world, giving us the compute to build stronger models that are also more economical to run.

This means we can provide customers with more capable models at lower cost. Grok 4.6, which we released Wednesday, provides an early look at what we can now build together. SpaceX is building the computing capacity needed to scale intelligence far beyond what exists today. Cursor will be one place where that intelligence becomes useful.

For us, that opens a much larger horizon than the one we started with, while keeping the work familiar. We still want to help people with ambitious ideas spend less time writing code and more time solving harder problems.
Article Summary: Cursor has officially been acquired by SpaceX. This completes the acquisition process that started in April. Cursor has gone from completing the next few lines of code to building AI teammates that you can give real work to. SpaceX is building the computing capacity needed to scale intelligence.

Article Title: Zerodha founder Nithin Kamath to startup founders: Stop saying 'we use AI'; 'Bragging that your product uses AI is like …’
Article Text:
Zerodha founder Nithin Kamath

Nithin Kamath says AI is now 'table stakes'

'Opening your pitch with AI' may hurt startup founders

Zerodha founder Nithin Kamath has shared a post with a message for startup founders trying to impress investors with AI. In a post on X, Nithin Kamath said he has become tired of seeing investment pitch decks that begin by highlighting AI, arguing that using AI is no longer a unique selling point. According to Kamath, AI has become so common that leading a presentation with "we use AI" is more likely to turn investors away than attract them. He said that “bragging that your product uses AI is like bragging that you take a bath every day”.Sharing his views, Kamath said the number of startup presentations that begin by talking about AI has become excessive. "The number of investment decks I get leading with 'we use AI' is ridiculous. It's reached a point where it automatically makes my eyes roll, and I've almost stopped looking at them," Kamath wrote.He said founders should understand that AI is no longer a competitive advantage by itself. "Founders need to realize that AI is just table stakes now. Bragging that your product uses AI is like bragging that you take a bath every day. It's not a differentiator."According to Kamath, simply saying a product uses AI does not explain why customers or investors should care.In the post, Nithin Kamath warned that making AI the first thing investors hear could have the opposite effect. "In fact, opening your pitch with it is a surefire way to get ignored, not just by us, but by most serious VCs," he said.Kamath also pointed to another trend created by generative AI. He said AI tools have made it easier than ever for founders to create polished-looking presentations, but that has also made many startup pitches look and sound alike."Especially now that AI has democratized the ability to generate 'nice-looking' decks, the last thing you want to do is say the exact same generic things as every other founder using the exact same tools," he wrote.
Article Summary: Zerodha founder Nithin Kamath says AI is no longer a unique selling point. Leading a presentation with "we use AI" is more likely to turn investors away than attract them. Kamath: Bragging that your product uses AI is like bragging that you take a bath every day.

Article Title: France’s top court blocks social media ban for kids: Here is what the ruling said
Article Text:
Representative image

Concerns cited over privacy and age verification

France’s highest constitutional authority on Friday (August 14) struck down landmark legislation aimed at banning teenagers under the age of 15 from using social media platforms, ruling that the proposed restrictions disproportionately infringed upon constitutional rights to free expression and privacy. The decision delivers a notable setback to President Emmanuel Macron’s administration, which has prioritised tightening youth digital safety rules and reducing screen time among minors.According to a report by news agency Reuters, following the ruling, the Elysee Palace announced that Macron has instructed Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu to redraft the bill to address the court's constitutional concerns before the end of his term in early 2027.The contested legislation, passed by French lawmakers in July, would have prohibited minors under 15 from creating new accounts on platforms such as TikTok, Instagram, Snapchat and YouTube starting September 1. Additionally, the rules required tech companies to terminate existing accounts held by underage users within four months and mandate identity-based age verification mechanisms approved by France’s data privacy regulator.However, the Constitutional Council concluded that the measure failed to provide adequate statutory safeguards, saying that the broad prohibition excessively curtailed the constitutional freedom of communication and expression for young citizens. The Justices also noted that while the bill required all internet users to submit age verification, it did not define the strict conditions, legal limits and data protection boundaries required to protect personal privacy.“The Council holds that the contested provisions, on the one hand, disproportionately infringe upon the freedom of expression and communication and, on the other, fail to provide the legal safeguards necessary to ensure the right to respect for private life,” the ruling stated.The French initiative was part of a widening international movement to restrict youth access to algorithm-driven social feeds. Lawmakers in Paris sought to follow Australia, which passed a nationwide ban for minors under 16 in December, while regulators in China, Turkey, the United Arab Emirates and the European Union continue to introduce stricter age verification frameworks and child safety regulations.
Article Summary: France's highest constitutional authority struck down landmark legislation aimed at banning teenagers under the age of 15 from using social media platforms. The decision delivers a notable setback to President Emmanuel Macron’s administration, which has prioritised tightening youth digital safety rules and reducing screen time among minors.

Article Title: China’s Z.ai claims its new GLM-5.3 model is close to Anthropic’s Mythos 5 level in cybersecurity tests
Article Text:
Representative image

Tiered rollout and responsible disclosure

Chinese artificial intelligence (AI) startup Z.ai has announced that its upcoming open-source model, GLM-5.3, demonstrated vulnerability detection capabilities on par with Anthropic’s restricted cybersecurity model, Mythos 5. Citing internal benchmark data shared by the company, a news article by Reuters says that GLM-5.3 scored 84.5% on CyberGym, which is an industry benchmark evaluating a model's ability to review source code, detect security flaws, and verify their authenticity. In comparison, Z.ai reported an 83.8% score for Anthropic's Mythos 5.While the model showed parity in passive flaw detection, it trailed Anthropic’s model in active exploit generation. On the ExploitBench test, GLM-5.3 achieved a 54.4% score versus 78% for Mythos 5. In timed tests, GLM-5.3 completed 130 attack-development tasks over six hours, compared to 247 tasks logged by Mythos 5.Anthropic currently restricts access to Mythos—a specialized derivative of Claude Fable 5 with offensive safety guardrails removed, limiting deployment strictly to vetted corporate and institutional partners under its "Project Glasswing" initiative.Taking a hybrid approach, Z.ai stated it plans a public release of GLM-5.3 in roughly two weeks following safety audits. However, the startup confirmed that its most sensitive cybersecurity capabilities will remain restricted behind a "trusted access" vetting program for launch partners.Industry governance analysts pointed to the structured rollout as a milestone for domestic risk management."To the best of my knowledge, this is the first time a Chinese lab is publicly justifying a delayed open release of model weights with safety considerations. This shows that open-weight risk management practices in China are becoming more sophisticated,” said Gabriel Wagner, an AI governance researcher at Beijing-based consultancy Concordia AI.To prevent misuse, Z.ai added multi-layered guardrails to screen incoming prompts and train the system to refuse malicious requests while preserving functionality for authorized penetration testing and bug fixing.
Article Summary: Z.ai's GLM-5.3 demonstrated vulnerability detection capabilities on par with Anthropic’s restricted cybersecurity model, Mythos 5. Anthropic currently restricts access to Mythos with offensive safety guardrails removed, limiting deployment strictly to vetted corporate and institutional partners under its "Project Glasswing" initiative.

Article Title: Microsoft is ‘killing’ Mico, the Copilot mascot it launched last October
Article Text:
Microsoft killed Clippy once. It's just done it again with Mico

Clippy survived a decade. Mico didn't last a year

Group Chat, Podcasts and Deep Research die on August 18 too

Microsoft is pulling Mico, the animated yellow blob that has fronted Copilot Voice since last October, out of the assistant's voice mode. The character isn't being deleted outright—it's being shifted to Learn Live, Microsoft's voice-based study mode, where it will work as an animated tutor. Copilot Voice itself stays exactly where it is. You'll still be able to talk to the chatbot and get spoken replies. You just won't have a blob pulling faces at you while you do it.The change was spotted on a Microsoft support page and reported by The Verge, and it lands as part of a much bigger housekeeping exercise. Microsoft is merging its consumer Copilot app with the Microsoft 365 Copilot app, and account updates begin rolling out from August 18, 2026. Mico goes in waves rather than on a single date, so your account may lose it before or after someone else's.Mico arrived in the Copilot Fall Release in October 2025, with Microsoft AI chief Mustafa Suleyman positioning it as a way to give the assistant an identity. It changed colour, reacted in real time, and was meant to make voice conversations feel less like talking to a spreadsheet. Microsoft's support page now says the character taught it about warmth, expressiveness, and how people want to talk with AI, and that Learn is where it has the most room to grow.That puts Mico in familiar company. Clippy shipped with Office 97 and was gone by Office 2007. Cortana ran from 2014 until its standalone app was retired in 2023. Rover and Bob went the same way in the nineties.Mico isn't the only casualty. Group Chat, Podcasts, Copilot Labs and consumer Deep Research all retire that day. Paid professional users get a tool called Researcher in place of Deep Research.There's a small amount of homework here. Existing Group Chats migrate as individual conversations, but messages, images and files uploaded by other participants won't come across, so download anything you want to keep first. Podcasts can be saved individually before the cutoff. And if you spent time customising your Mico's colours and looks, Microsoft's advice: take a screenshot, because those settings don't travel to Learn Live.
Article Summary: Mico, the animated yellow blob that has fronted Copilot Voice since last October, is being moved to Learn Live, Microsoft's voice-based study mode. Group Chat, Podcasts, Copilot Labs and consumer Deep Research all retire on August 18, 2026.
